757.title: The soul of the world
757.hook: an old letter to a man called Diognetus says Christians live in their own countries as sojourners, and are to the world what the soul is to the body
757.carry: every homeland foreign, every foreign land home
757.howItsDone: Some Christians draw on the letter to Diognetus and on 1 Peter's 'strangers and pilgrims' when they talk about belonging to a city while also belonging to God, and some churches pray for their towns and local leaders in their services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Polycarp, the old bishop who served Christ eighty-six years and would not curse him. Your line: eighty-six years.

A man named Diognetus has questions. Who are these Christians? What God do they trust? Why don't they fear death, and why do they love each other like that? Somebody writes him an answer, and doesn't sign it. We learn little about Diognetus, either. The letter describes the Christians around it the way you'd describe neighbors to a visitor. They don't live in their own cities or speak a special language. They eat the ordinary food and wear the ordinary clothes of wherever they live. You couldn't pick them out in a crowd. Then the letter says something strange about where they belong.

In paraphrase: Christians live in their own countries, but as sojourners. They take part in everything as citizens and put up with everything as foreigners. Every foreign land is a homeland to them, and every homeland a foreign land. They marry and have children like everyone else. They obey the laws, and in their own lives go beyond them. Mistreated, they bless. The idea is older than the letter. The first letter of Peter, in the King James Bible, writes to believers "as strangers and pilgrims." Hebrews says the faithful of old "confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth." The letter turns that idea into a way of living in a city. Then its boldest picture: what the soul is to the body, Christians are to the world. The soul is spread through every part of the body, and Christians through every city. The soul lives in the body but isn't of it. The body even resents the soul, and still the soul holds it together. Some readers find that claim too big for any group to live up to. Others hear it as a job description, not a boast: be in the city, care for the city, and don't let it be the whole of you. The prophet Jeremiah had told exiles in Babylon, "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives." Stranger and citizen at once.
screen: `WHAT THE SOUL IS TO THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Picture the place you live, your street, your building, your town, and name one small, ordinary thing you could do for it, like checking on a neighbor. Then notice one way the place pulls at you that you'd rather not follow, and hold both. If you pray, name your town to God, street by street; if you don't, simply wish it well.
Diognetus. The man whose questions prompted a letter saying what the soul is to the body, Christians are to the world: spread through it, holding it together, never quite at home.
Your line: every homeland foreign, every foreign land home. In the city, and never only of it. See you tomorrow.

758.title: Sunday in AD 150
758.hook: a teacher named Justin explains Christian worship to the emperor: readings, a sermon, prayers, bread and wine, and a collection for widows
758.howItsDone: Christian Sunday services can include readings from scripture, preaching, prayers and an offering; churches differ on how often they share communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the letter to Diognetus: Christians as citizens and sojourners, the soul of the world. Your line: every homeland foreign, every foreign land home.
screen: `EVERY HOMELAND FOREIGN, EVERY FOREIGN LAND HOME.`

segments.voice: Rumors travel fast about people who meet behind closed doors. So a Christian teacher named Justin does something brave: he writes a defense of his faith and addresses it to the emperor himself. Near the end, he stops arguing and simply describes what Christians do when they gather. No secret rites, nothing hidden. Just the order of a morning. Tradition remembers him as Justin Martyr, and his description opens a window onto a Christian Sunday from a time when, as he complains, Christians were accused of things they never did.

In paraphrase: on the day called Sunday, everyone in the cities or out in the country gathers in one place. The memoirs of the apostles, his name for the gospel accounts, or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time allows. When the reader stops, the one presiding speaks, urging everyone to imitate these good things. Then all stand together and pray. Bread is brought, and wine mixed with water. The one presiding offers prayers and thanksgivings as well as he's able, and the people answer, Amen. Justin explains the word for the emperor: in Hebrew, he says, it means so be it. The bread and cup are shared, and the deacons carry some to those who couldn't come. This food, Justin says, is called eucharistia, thanksgiving, and only the baptized share it. Then the collection. Those with plenty give what they choose, and the one presiding uses it for orphans and widows, the sick, those in prison, and strangers passing through. Why Sunday? Two reasons: it's the first day, when God began making the world out of darkness, and the day Jesus Christ rose from the dead. Readings, a sermon, standing to pray, bread and cup, Amen, an offering. Churches today arrange the pieces differently, and share the bread and cup more or less often, but the pieces are recognizable. And notice where the collection goes. Not to the building. To widows, prisoners and strangers.
screen: `STAND AND PRAY, THEN BREAD AND CUP.`

segments.voice: Picture that plain room: people from the city and from the fields, someone reading for as long as there's time, everyone standing to pray, bread and a cup going around, a few pieces wrapped up for someone sick at home. Notice who's in the room, and who isn't, and who's being remembered. If you pray, join their Amen; if you don't, let the picture be strange and familiar at once.

759.title: Perpetua and Felicity
759.hook: a young noblewoman and an enslaved woman, both new mothers, face the arena together, and one reaches out a hand to lift the other
759.howItsDone: Christians who keep a calendar of saints remember Perpetua and Felicity together, on one day, and their story is sometimes read or preached then.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Justin's Sunday in his own words: readings, a sermon, bread and cup, and a collection for strangers. Your line: on the day called sunday.

A father is on his knees in a prison in Carthage, in North Africa, begging his daughter. Have pity on my gray hair. Have pity on your mother, your brothers, your baby son, who won't live without you. His daughter is Vibia Perpetua: well born, educated, a new mother nursing her child in a cell. She has been arrested as a Christian. All she has to do is say she isn't one. And for a long stretch of the account, the words are Perpetua's own: her prison diary, in the first person, kept by the people who loved her.
screen: `ALL SHE HAS TO DO IS DENY IT.`

segments.voice: Perpetua answers her father with a water jug. She points to one lying nearby: can that be called by any other name than what it is? No, he says. So, she says, I can't call myself anything other than what I am, a Christian. In prison with her is Felicity, an enslaved woman, heavily pregnant. Felicity's fear is a quiet one: that her pregnancy will hold back her execution, and she'll die later, without her friends, among common criminals. The others pray with her, and she goes into labor in the prison. She gives birth to a daughter, and a Christian woman takes the baby to raise as her own. Now there are two new mothers, one free and well born, one enslaved: nothing in common by the rules of their city, everything in common by the rules of their faith. In the arena, the account says, a wild cow throws the two women down. Perpetua gets up first. She sees Felicity on the ground, goes to her, gives her her hand, and lifts her up, and the two stand together. Before the end, the martyrs give one another the kiss of peace. Churches that remember them still name them side by side, the noblewoman and the slave. Some readers notice the small things the account keeps: a jug, a father's gray hair, a woman pinning up her hair in the arena. It reads less like a legend about saints than a diary about people.
screen: `A WATER JUG: I AM WHAT I AM.`
`SHE GAVE HER HAND AND LIFTED HER UP.`

segments.voice: If someone is beside you, take their hand for this minute, without needing to explain. If you're alone, rest one hand in the other, bring to mind someone who's been knocked down lately, and picture going to them and lifting them up. If you pray, hold them in prayer; if not, hold the picture of the two of you standing together.

Your line: sisters. A free woman and an enslaved one, standing up together. Until tomorrow.

760.title: Fully alive
760.hook: Irenaeus: the glory of God is a human being fully alive
760.carry: awake, creative, glad to be in a body
760.howItsDone: Some Christians quote Irenaeus's line in sermons, retreats and books about prayer and creativity, and some pair it with its second half, that the life of a human being is the vision of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christiana sum, Perpetua's answer, and two women standing together. Your line: sisters.

A few days ago we met Polycarp, the old bishop who wouldn't curse Christ. A man named Irenaeus writes that he saw Polycarp in his own early youth, and remembers him. Irenaeus grows up to be a bishop himself, and writes a long, careful book against teachings he believes are pulling Christians away from the faith they received. It's big and argumentative, full of names and systems. And somewhere in the middle sits one short line that people still quote today.

In its old Latin text, the line reads gloria Dei vivens homo. Word for word: the glory of God, a living human being. Some modern versions say: the glory of God is a human being fully alive. Fully alive is a translator's way of bringing out vivens, living; they aren't separate words in the Latin. And the sentence goes on. In paraphrase: and the life of a human being is the vision of God. So it's a circle. God is glorified when people are truly alive, and people are truly alive when they see God. Why say it? Some teachers in Irenaeus's world taught that the physical world was a mistake, that the body was a prison, and that real spiritual life meant escaping it. Irenaeus pushes back hard. The one God made the world, and made it good. God works with dust and breath, and the Son of God took on flesh. It's the note the Bible strikes in its first chapter: "God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." For Irenaeus, being human isn't a problem to be solved. It's what God is bringing to life. Christians hear the line in different ways. Some hear joy: God delights in people who are awake, creative, glad to be in a body. Others quickly add the second half, so fully alive never just means busy or thrilled; for Irenaeus, the deepest life is seeing God. Both halves belong to the one sentence.
screen: `AND THE LIFE OF HUMANS: SEEING GOD.`

segments.voice: Notice that you're in a body: feet, hands, the weight of you in the chair. Then let your mind go to something that makes you more yourself, not just busy, like cooking for people, walking under trees, singing badly or fixing a thing. If you pray, offer it to God as a thank you; if you don't, just hold it, and look forward to it.

Your line: awake, creative, glad to be in a body. And the other half: seeing God. That's day seven hundred sixty.

761.title: The fish sign
761.hook: a fish, two curved lines: in Greek, its letters spell the initials of Jesus Christ, God's Son, Savior
761.howItsDone: Some Christians use the fish symbol on jewelry, cars, signs and church art as a quiet sign of faith, and some teach children the five Greek words behind it.

segments.voice: Fully alive, yesterday's word, from Irenaeus: the glory of God is a living human being, and the life of a human being is seeing God. Your line: awake, creative, glad to be in a body.
screen: `AWAKE, CREATIVE, GLAD TO BE IN A BODY.`

segments.voice: Two curved lines, crossing at one end. A child can draw it in the sand. It turns up on the backs of cars, on necklaces, on bakery signs and business cards, telling you, roughly, that somebody here is a Christian. But why a fish? It isn't a cross, a lamb or a dove. It's lunch. And the answer is a word puzzle, hidden in plain sight, in Greek.

The Greek word for fish is ichthys. Five letters: iota, chi, theta, upsilon, sigma. Take each as the first letter of a word, and you get a creed. Iesous: Jesus. Christos: Christ. Theou: of God. Huios: Son. Soter: Savior. Jesus Christ, God's Son, Savior. Augustine, in the City of God, spells out the five Greek words, says their first letters make ichthys, fish, and that Christ is understood in the word. Then he adds a picture: Christ could live without sin in the deep waters of this mortal life, the way a fish lives in the depths. Earlier still, a North African writer named Tertullian makes the fish a picture of baptism. In his book on baptism he calls Christians little fishes, born in water, following our Ichthys, Jesus Christ. And fish swim through the Gospels too. Jesus calls fishermen: "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." He feeds crowds with loaves and fishes. After the resurrection, in John's Gospel, he cooks fish on a beach for his friends. Now, the secret part. Tradition says early Christians scratched the fish on walls and tombs. And there's a story told today: in times of danger, one stranger would draw one curve in the dust, and if the other drew the second, they knew they were safe together. It's a good story, but the ancient writers quoted here don't tell it. What they show is a sign explained openly, in books anyone could read. A secret, maybe, the way a family's private joke is: you have to be inside to get it.

With a finger on the table, a pen on paper, or in the air, draw one curve, then the other, crossing at the tail, and trace it slowly, again and again. Let the five words go by with it if you like: Jesus, Christ, God's, Son, Savior. If you pray, those five words can be your prayer, nothing added; if not, keep tracing, and notice how small a thing can carry a whole meaning.
Ichthys. Greek for fish. Its five letters begin five words: Jesus Christ, God's Son, Savior.
Your line: the secret sign. Five Greek letters, and a whole creed inside them. Rest easy.

762.title: Seed of the church
762.hook: Tertullian tells the rulers of Rome that every time they cut Christians down, more grow back
762.howItsDone: Some churches set aside prayers for Christians persecuted for their faith, and Tertullian's seed line is sometimes quoted when they do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ichthys, the Greek for fish: five letters, five words, Jesus Christ, God's Son, Savior. Your line: the secret sign.

If the Tiber floods the city, blame the Christians. If the Nile doesn't rise to the fields, blame the Christians. If the earth shakes, if there's famine or plague, the cry goes up at once: Christians to the lion. That's how Tertullian, a fierce, sharp-tongued writer from Carthage in North Africa, describes the mood around him, in a defense of his faith addressed to the rulers of the Roman world. He's writing for people who are being arrested, tortured and killed. And at the very end, instead of pleading, he says something that sounds almost like a dare.

In paraphrase: go on, Tertullian tells the governors. Torture us, condemn us, grind us down. Your cruelty proves we're innocent, and it does you no good. The more often you mow us down, the more of us there are. The blood of Christians is seed. Not the end of something; the beginning. The version people quote today is smoother: the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church. Tertullian's own line is shorter, and blunter. Why seed? Some readers hear an echo of Paul, writing to Corinth about the resurrection, in the King James Bible: "that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die." A seed kept safe in a jar stays a seed. One that goes into the dark ground can become a field. Tertullian also says why it works. People watch Christians stand firm and start asking: what makes them like this? Some who ask, he says, end up joining them. The very thing meant to end the church starts conversations. Some readers add a careful word: Tertullian was making a bold claim to the people persecuting him, not stating a law of history, and the line can sound cold to Christians suffering for their faith today. Others hold onto it exactly for them: it refuses to let the persecutor decide what those lives meant. Either way, a seed in the ground looks like loss. Nobody standing over it can see the field.
screen: `THE MORE YOU MOW US DOWN, THE MORE WE GROW.`
`A BOLD CLAIM, NOT A LAW OF HISTORY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind people anywhere in the world who are mocked, jailed or threatened today for what they believe, Christians and people of other faiths too; you don't need names, and if you know one story, hold that one. If you pray, pray for them in your own way, or simply say their situation to God and leave it there. If you don't, hold them steadily in your attention for this minute, without turning away.

763.title: Origen reading
763.hook: a scholar and teacher of the young who read scripture on more than one level: body, soul and spirit
763.howItsDone: Some Christians read scripture both for its plain meaning and for what it says to their lives and about God; monastic communities and some prayer groups practice slow, layered reading of a short passage, called lectio divina.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tertullian's dare: the more you mow us down, the more we grow. Your line: seed, not end.

A teenage boy in Alexandria wants to run out and die beside his father, arrested as a Christian. His mother can't talk him out of it. So, the story goes, she hides all his clothes. That's how the church historian Eusebius begins Origen's life. The boy writes his father a letter instead, urging him to hold firm. His father is killed, and the family is left with nothing. And the boy who couldn't leave the house becomes, while still young, the teacher of people preparing for baptism, and a reader of the Bible people still learn from and argue with.

Origen's big idea: scripture is built like a person. A human being, he says, has a body, a soul and a spirit, and so does the Bible. The body is the plain story, the words as they stand, and that alone helps simpler readers. The soul is what the text says to how you live: your choices, your habits, your heart. The spirit is what it shows about God and Christ and the life to come. Not every reader is ready for every level, he says, and that's fine. Then a bolder move. Sometimes, he says, the text puts a stumbling block in the plain story on purpose, something that can't work if you take it flatly, to make you look deeper. His example: Genesis counts a first day, a second, a third, with evening and morning, before it mentions the sun and moon. How can there be days with no sun? For Origen, the puzzle is a door, not a mistake. Christians still differ here: some read Genesis closely as history, some as Origen did, others hold the plain story and the deeper meaning together. And some of Origen's other ideas were later disputed, so churches still differ on how to remember him. But his habit of reading echoes. Whenever a preacher says this story is about Israel and also about you, that's what Origen spent his life on. Ask what a verse says, then what it says to you, then what it says about God.

Here's a short verse from the Psalms, in the King James Bible: "Be still, and know that I am God." Read it three ways, slowly: its body, what it simply says; its soul, where you're not still today; its spirit, what it says about God. If you pray, let the verse be the prayer; if you don't, let it be a sentence you turn over in your hands.
Origen reading. A way of reading scripture on three levels, like a person: body, soul and spirit. The plain story, the life, and God.
Your line: read deeper. A letter, a Sunday, two sisters, a living human being, a fish, a seed and a reader: that was the week. Week one hundred nine, done.
